The research on whether cameras reduce crime is genuinely divided. [d3] A meta-analysis of 93 studies found surveillance systems most effective in parking lots (51% decrease in crime), but results in city centers and public housing showed only a 7% decrease that was not statistically significant, and the drop in countries outside the UK was largely insignificant. [d2] The UK College of Policing's crime reduction toolkit concludes there is overall evidence that CCTV reduces crime, but also notes that "CCTV implemented on its own or alongside one other intervention did not have a statistically significant effect in reducing crime," with success tied to coverage, context, and implementation quality. [d5] By contrast, a British Home Office review of dozens of studies found that half showed a negative or negligible effect and the other half showed a negligible decrease of 4% at most; crime in Glasgow actually increased by 9% after cameras were installed, and Tampa's facial recognition program failed to result in a single arrest, leading experts to argue that cameras are forensic tools rather than crime prevention tools. [d1] Some analyses do report positive outcomes in specific settings—such as a 37% crime reduction in car parks and 12% in residential areas—but acknowledge that violent crime was not affected by camera presence. [d4] A Cobb County LPR camera program reported a 35% total crime drop after one year, though this is a single program case study. [d6] Research on taxicab cameras suggests cameras deter crime when properly used and publicized, but only when cameras are functioning and their presence is known to potential offenders.
